query: For high-entropy nanoalloys in high-temperature applications, what governs structural and chemical stability, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, propose a controlled comparison that would distinguish it from alternatives, predict observations relative to a baseline, define the boundaries of the prediction, identify supporting evidence from the background, and state a falsifying outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In situ transmission electron microscopy (TEM) or X-ray diffraction (XRD) reveals that the structural and chemical stability of high-entropy nanoalloys in high-temperature applications is governed by the formation of a single phase, such as a body-centered cubic (bcc) or face-centered cubic (fcc) phase, which is stabilized by the high configurational entropy of the alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy nanoalloys with a composition of multiple principal elements, such as W, Mo, Ta, Nb, or Ni, in approximately equimolar ratios.
generation.intervention: In situ TEM or XRD characterization of the alloy's microstructure and phase formation during high-temperature applications.
generation.conditions: High-temperature environment, such as those encountered in aerospace or chemical industry applications.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a single phase, such as a bcc or fcc phase, which is stabilized by the high configurational entropy of the alloy.
generation.mechanism: The high configurational entropy of the alloy increases with increasing temperature, stabilizing the formation of a single phase and preventing the formation of multiple phases or segregation of alloying elements.
generation.predicted_outcome: The high-entropy nanoalloy will exhibit improved structural and chemical stability, including increased resistance to oxidation and fatigue, at high temperatures.
generation.baseline: Conventional alloys with a single principal element, which may exhibit reduced stability and increased degradation at high temperatures.
generation.boundary: The prediction is limited to high-entropy nanoalloys with a composition of multiple principal elements in approximately equimolar ratios, and may not apply to alloys with significantly different compositions or microstructures.
generation.uncertainty: The exact mechanism by which the high configurational entropy stabilizes the formation of a single phase is not fully understood, and further research is needed to elucidate the underlying atomic-scale processes.

falsification_experiment.design: In situ TEM or XRD characterization of a high-entropy nanoalloy with a composition that is predicted to form multiple phases or exhibit reduced stability at high temperatures.
measurements: Chemical composition and segregation of alloying elements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy exhibits reduced stability or forms multiple phases at high temperatures, the hypothesis is falsified.

It is found from the RBA calculations that competition between the FCC and B2 phases starts at valence electron concentration, n ≈ 8. Comparison with the present experimental data for CCFN-Al0.5 (n = 7.67) where FCC peaks are indicated in XRD (Fig. IIc), shows that the RBA model may overestimate the stability of the B2 phase. However, in comparison with a new HEA composition, AlCoCrFeNi2.1, where the corresponding valence electron concentration is n = 7.70, the experimental observation of an FCC/B2 dual-phase constitution. Furthermore, experimental evidence of B2 presence has also been reported in CCFN-Al0.75, CCFN-Al1, and CCFN-Al1.5 with n values ranging from 6.57 to 7.41. These observations not only validate our theoretical prediction but also demonstrate that the formation of B2 phase is strongly correlated with the short-range chemical order between Al and the excess composition of Ni transition metals in the HEAs, suggesting possible effects of the processing method and cooling rate, as noted by Dahlborg et al..

One of the major challenges of near-equiatomic NiTi shape memory alloys is their limitation for high-temperature applications. To overcome this barrier, researchers have tried to enhance the transformation temperatures by addition of alloying elements or even by introducing the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs). In this study, the CuNiHfTiZr HEAs were developed for high-temperature shape memory effect. Based on their solubility and electron configurations, the alloying elements are divided into two groups, (CuNi)50 and (HfTiZr)50. The content of Cu in (CuNi)50 is modulated to investigate the influences of Cu on martensitic transformation of the HEAs by studying structural evolution and transformation behavior. The results of x-ray diffraction and thermal expansion tests revealed that Cu15Ni35Hf16.67Ti16.67Zr16.67 possesses high transformation temperature, narrow hysteresis temperature loops, and good dimensional stability within this HEA system.

In situ TEM experiments reveal the crystalline-to-amorphous phase transformation in an ultrafine-grained Cantor alloy. AbstractThe Cantor high-entropy alloy (HEA) of CrMnFeCoNi is a solid solution with a face-centered cubic structure. While plastic deformation in this alloy is usually dominated by dislocation slip and deformation twinning, our in situ straining transmission electron microscopy (TEM) experiments reveal a crystalline-to-amorphous phase transformation in an ultrafine-grained Cantor alloy. We find that the crack-tip structural evolution involves a sequence of formation of the crystalline, lamellar, spotted, and amorphous patterns, which represent different proportions and organizations of the crystalline and amorphous phases. Such solid-state amorphization stems from both the high lattice friction and high grain boundary resistance to dislocation glide in ultrafine-grained microstructures. The resulting increase of crack-tip dislocation densities promotes the buildup of high stresses for triggering the crystalline-to-amorphous transformation. High entropy or multi principal element alloys are a promising and relatively young concept for designing alloys. The idea of creating alloys without a single main alloying element opens up a wide space for possible new alloy compositions. High entropy alloys based on refractory metals such as W, Mo, Ta or Nb are of interest for future high temperature applications e.g., in the aerospace or chemical industry. However, producing refractory metal high entropy alloys by conventional metallurgical methods remains challenging. For this reason, the feasibility of laser-based additive manufacturing of the refractory metal high entropy alloy W20Mo20Ta20Nb20V20 by laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB/M) is investigated in the present work. In-situ alloy formation from mixtures of easily available elemental powders is employed to avoid an expensive atomization of pre-alloyed powder. It is shown that PBF-LB/M of W20Mo20Ta20Nb20V20 is in general possible and that a complete fusion of the powder mixture without a significant number of undissolved particles is achievable by in-situ alloy formation during PBF-LB/M when selecting favorable process parameter combinations.
